newsitem.title: UK: Minor Metals - Bismuth and cobalt stable.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals - Bismuth and cobalt stable.

text.p: Bismuth and cobalt remained steady over the last week, while conditions elsewhere in the minor metals sector remained sluggish, traders said.
Meeting some consumer resistance bismuth failed to hit its upside target of $4.00 a pound, though traders believed this level would soon be reached against the backdrop of low stocks.
A lack of Peruvian and Mexican stocks helped to underpin the metal which can be used in shot gun pellets and pharmaceuticals.

In a article for Reuter's Frank Fauche managing director of trade house Ferromin Ltd said bismuth is looking for a new trading range between $4.00 and $5.00 a pound if consumers start to rebuild inventories.
In a longer term view Fauche said it was not unreasonable to expect wild swings between $5.00 and $10.00 if new supplies do not come on stream in the next few years.

While agreeing with levels of around $4.00 a pound one European trader said he doubted prices would move much higher near-term. Despite talk that China has little available material the trader said they would be tempted to sell at around $4.00.
He saw bismuth trading in a range of between $3.40/$3.60 or $3.50/$3.70.
The trader also believed the long term price direction was in the hands of the producers. "They do not want a volatile market," he commented.
Several traders remained bullish to cobalt despite the ending of the seven month civil war in Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Despite pressure from consumers several London traders said they were not prepared to mark the price of cobalt lower as they saw the ending of Mobutu's rule as only a psychological influence.

It will take a long time to repair facilities neglected by the Mobutu regime, and planned new mines/smelters, like the giant Tenke Fungurume venture, won't be making a difference to production levels for two to three years, traders said.
Reports from Lubumbashi said that Zambia stopped cross-border railway traffic this month because of a dispute over debts. The main export route for Zaire's cobalt is to South Africa via Zambia.
"Zambia has blocked all the wagons and goods of Congolese (Zaire's) clients. We've asked them to lift this embargo," a Zairean official told Reuters in an interview.

Cobalt was underpinned by news that the DLA could not yet resume cobalt sales as Minor Metals Inc in its recent U.S. court case had been granted a preliminary injunction preventing the Stockpile from going ahead with its one-million pound March solicitation.
The court ordered parties to confer and report back as to how they wish to proceed by June 13.

One trader said that the DLA has effectively frozen out a minimum of 2.7 million pounds of cobalt in their financial year to 30 September. The DLA have to give a minimum of 30 days notice. The earliest the tender could take place would be mid-July.
Global stocks of cobalt remain low while demand is brisk, the trader noted.
Elsewhere, cadmium held steady but the recent buying was said to have started to dry up.

Gallium also held steady on talk that major producer Russia had withdrawn two shipments. Germanium was under pressure from oversupply and was forecast to drop soon. "There is a big drop on the cards," one trader commented.
